To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the progenitor set for early-type galaxies in a standard LCDM model is a function of the present-day stellar mass of the galaxy, and that the “red sequence”, defined as the colour–magnitude locus dominated by early-type galaxies, does not trace the progenitor population of early-types at low stellar masses.

(1) the progenitor set for present-day early-types is dominated by late-type objects, (2) the progenitor bias is a strong function of both the mass of the galaxy and the epoch of observation, and (3) the “red sequence”, defined as the part of the B −V vs. MV plane that is populated by early-types, does not trace the progenitor-set of early-types at fainter luminosity.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what is the true progenitor set of early-type galaxies in a LCDM universe?
a fundamental question in galaxy evolution: what is the origin of early-type galaxies?
the question of how well the progenitors of the present-day E/S0 population are represented in the current observational data sets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the progenitors of the present-day E/S0 population are a mix of red and blue galaxies, with the exact mix depending on the luminosity range under consideration.
the progenitors of early-type galaxies are not exclusively early-type galaxies, but rather a mixed set of early-type and spiral galaxies, with a higher fraction of the former at higher redshifts.
, while the red-sequence is a reasonable approximation for the progenitor set for massive galaxies, it breaks down at faint luminosities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the standard model predicts that, at a given redshift, the majority of the early-type progenitor galaxies have a spiral-like appearance, while the fraction of early-type progenitors among the blue spiral galaxies is significantly lower than among the red spiral galaxies.
we can identify the progenitors of the early-type galaxy population at any redshift, and we can also predict the fraction of the progenitor galaxies which are late-type.

the standard LCDM model can explain most, if not all, of the observed properties of early-types, and the results of the present work provide a useful guide to interpreting the results of future observational studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when studying the evolution of early-type galaxies in a semi-analytic context, it is essential to consider the entire “progenitor population”, which includes both early- and late-type progenitors.

, in the standard model, a substantial fraction of the progenitors that contribute significantly to the build-up of the early-type stellar mass density are late-type galaxies, and that these progenitors should be accounted for when studying the evolution of the present-day population of early-type galaxies.

, while the red sequence can provide a good tracer of the progenitor set for massive galaxies, it is not an appropriate tracer of the progenitors for fainter systems, and that the progenitor set is not well defined in colour–magnitude space.
